cards.title: Numbers you can share
cards.idea: Four friends split 3 rotis equally. Each share is 3/4 of a roti — a number written as one whole over another.

interaction.prompt: Tap the roti to cut it into equal shares

cards.reveal: 3 rotis shared by 4 gives 3/4 each. Any amount you can write as p/q, with whole numbers p and q (q not zero), is a rational number.

cards.title: Every fraction is a dot
cards.idea: Slide a point along the number line. Fractions like 1/2, 3/4, 7/5 all land at exact spots between the whole numbers.

interaction.prompt: Slide to place the fraction on the line

cards.reveal: Between any two whole numbers sit endless rationals. You can always halve the gap and find another fraction.

interaction.prompt: Slide the point to one half

stages.reveal: At 0.5 the point sits exactly halfway. This is 1/2, a rational number.
stages.caption: Every fraction has its own exact home on the line.

cards.title: Decimals that settle or repeat
cards.idea: Divide to turn a fraction into a decimal. 1/4 = 0.25 stops; 1/3 = 0.333... repeats forever in a pattern.

interaction.prompt: Tap each fraction to see its decimal

cards.reveal: Rational numbers always give decimals that either terminate or repeat a block endlessly. The pattern never fully vanishes.

cards.title: A length with no fraction
cards.idea: Draw a square of side 1. Its diagonal has length √2 — a number no fraction p/q can equal.

interaction.prompt: Tap the diagonal of the unit square

cards.reveal: √2 = 1.41421356... its decimal never ends and never repeats. It cannot be written as p/q, so it is irrational.

imageSpec.subject: a unit square with its diagonal drawn and labelled root two
imageSpec.caption: The diagonal of a 1 by 1 square is √2, an irrational length.

derivation.label: the diagonal of a unit square

steps.note: each side is 1, by the Pythagoras relation
which is 1.41421..., a non-terminating non-repeating decimal

cards.title: Name the two families
cards.idea: Rational: can be written p/q, decimal terminates or repeats. Irrational: cannot be written p/q, decimal never ends and never repeats.

interaction.prompt: Tap a number to sort it into its family

cards.reveal: Together, rationals and irrationals fill the whole number line with no gaps. This complete set is called the real numbers.

cards.title: Sorting the tricky ones
cards.idea: Is 0.101001000... rational? Its pattern grows, so it never truly repeats a fixed block. That makes it irrational.

interaction.prompt: Tap the numbers that are irrational

cards.reveal: √4 = 2 is rational, but √3 and π are irrational. Look for a repeating or ending decimal to spot a rational.

chapters.title: What rational means
chapters.script: A rational number is any number you can write as p over q, where p and q are whole numbers and q is not zero. Simple fractions like three quarters, whole numbers like five, and decimals that stop or repeat are all rational. When you divide, the decimal either ends, like one quarter being nought point two five, or it settles into a repeating block, like one third being nought point three, three, three forever.

chapters.title: What irrational means
chapters.script: Some numbers cannot be written as p over q at all. The diagonal of a one by one square, root two, is the classic example. Its decimal, one point four one four two and on, never ends and never repeats. Pi, from circles, is the same. These are irrational numbers. Together with the rationals they fill the number line completely, and we call the whole collection the real numbers.
